lesson.title: The Second Derivative Test's Blind Spot: What to Do When f''(c) Equals Zero
lesson.summary: The second derivative test is fast, but it goes silent exactly when f''(c) equals zero. Work through one case where the point turns out to be a minimum anyway and one where it is neither, then fall back on the first derivative test.
lesson.body:
The Second Derivative Test used throughout the last two chapters is a convenient shortcut: check the sign of f''(c), and read off whether the critical point is a maximum or a minimum without needing to test values on either side. But the test has a real blind spot. When f''(c) = 0, it gives no information at all, not "probably a max," not "probably a min," genuinely nothing. Treating a zero second derivative as if it settles the question is a common and avoidable mistake.

Consider f(x) = x^4. Differentiate: f'(x) = 4x^3, and setting this to zero gives x = 0 as the only critical point. Differentiate again: f''(x) = 12x^2, so f''(0) = 0. The Second Derivative Test is inconclusive here, it simply cannot tell you whether x = 0 is a max, a min, or neither.

Fall back on the First Derivative Test instead. For x < 0, take x = -1: f'(-1) = 4(-1)^3 = -4, which is negative, so the function is falling. For x > 0, take x = 1: f'(1) = 4(1)^3 = 4, which is positive, so the function is rising. The sign changes from negative to positive, which confirms x = 0 is a local minimum, in fact the global minimum, f(0) = 0, even though the second derivative test had nothing to say about it.

Now compare a second example where the same inconclusive situation leads to a completely different outcome. Consider f(x) = x^3. Differentiate: f'(x) = 3x^2, with a critical point at x = 0. Differentiate again: f''(x) = 6x, so f''(0) = 0, inconclusive again. Apply the First Derivative Test: for x < 0, take x = -1: f'(-1) = 3(-1)^2 = 3, positive. For x > 0, take x = 1: f'(1) = 3(1)^2 = 3, also positive. There is no sign change at all, the derivative is positive on both sides. That means x = 0 is neither a local maximum nor a local minimum, the function simply flattens out for an instant while continuing to rise through what is called an inflection point.

The lesson is not that f''(c) = 0 secretly always means one particular outcome, it is that f''(c) = 0 means the second derivative test cannot be used at all, and the sign pattern of the first derivative on either side of c must be checked directly, by hand, before drawing any conclusion.

In applied optimization problems this exact blind spot shows up less often than in pure algebra exercises, because most physical objective functions, areas, volumes, costs, tend to be built from polynomials or rational functions whose second derivatives keep a single consistent sign across the whole practical domain. The can problem from earlier in this unit is a good example: S''(r) = 4 pi + 4V/r^3 is positive for every single r > 0 in the domain, with no exceptions to worry about. Still, whenever a second derivative does evaluate to zero at a critical point, the correct response is always the same, switch to the First Derivative Test rather than guessing.
